summary: This is the answer to AC-4 of EVENTS-005, handed over so the database lane is not left to guess, and the answer is NEGATIVE: public.event_claims does NOT follow public.events_v2, and the forward discriminator migration the task record anticipated is NOT owed. DECIDED 2026-09-28 by the events lane, which owns the claim product surface. THE ANSWER, AND WHY IT IS NOT A DEFECT TO MIGRATE AWAY. A claim transfers ownership of an event that HAS NONE. Four independent facts, all measured, say the claim subject is a `public.events` row and nothing else. (1) The code that creates the rows a claim is filed against says so in its own words: `lib/events/canonical-event-service.ts:125-128` inserts into `public.events` with `artist_id: null` and the comment 'Imported events have no owning artist user; ownership arrives via the claims flow'. That comment sits on the INSERT. (2) A canonical event cannot lack an owner: `supabase/migrations/20250816133000` creates `events_v2` with `created_by uuid not null references auth.users(id)` at line 51. There is no `events_v2` row in the schema that a claim could apply to. (3) The claim route independently encodes the same boundary, for the same reason, without reference to the FK: `app/api/events/[id]/claim/route.ts:52-54` returns `409 ALREADY_OWNED` whenever the event has an owner. (4) All three live consumers of `event_claims` read or write `public.events` — `claim/route.ts:47`, `tour/route.ts:26`, `admin/event-claims/route.ts:59` — so the FK and the call sites agree; the contract is coherent, not merely consistent by accident. CONSEQUENCE, STATED PLAINLY SO IT IS NOT RE-RAISED. The gap DB-023 measured — a claim against an id that is not a legacy `events` row is refused 23503, so a canonical `events_v2` event can never be claimed — is the CORRECT behaviour, not a limitation. It is the database correctly refusing to attach a provider-ingestion ownership transfer to an org-owned, natively-created event. The three parents are not three versions of one thing: `public.events` holds provider-imported unowned rows, `public.artist_events` holds creator-owned legacy rows, and `public.events_v2` holds Tourify-native org rows that are owned from creation. A claim names the first. A `event_table` discriminator on `event_claims` would make the table claim that all three are claimable, which is false for two of them, and would replace a real single-relation foreign key with a nullable discriminator column that nothing can enforce. THE MIGRATION THIS LANE WILL NOT ASK FOR. Had the answer been yes, the shape would have been: add `event_table text not null default 'events' check (event_table in ('events','events_v2'))`, drop the `event_id -> public.events(id)` FK (which cascades deletes and would have to be re-implemented per discriminator arm, or simply lost), and add a three-arm predicate to `event_claims_self_read` and `event_claims_self_insert`. That was NOT authored, per the task record's scope exclusion, and it is NOT being requested. WHAT THE SCHEMA WOULD OWE IF THE PRODUCT CHANGES ITS MIND. Only if Tourify decides that an org or venue should be able to claim a canonical `events_v2` event — a product decision that has NOT been made and is not implied by anything in the repository — would a discriminator become correct. That is new work with a new decision, and it belongs to the events lane's charter (`app/api/events/[id]/route.ts`, the events_v2 lifecycle handler, is EVENTS-001's and is blocked). It is named here so the database lane does not discover it as a surprise.
